newsitem.title: USA: Dlr ends off in US on EMU talk, Sakakibara remarks.
newsitem.headline: Dlr ends off in US on EMU talk, Sakakibara remarks.

text.p: The dollar ended lower as the mark gained on talk that Italy will be excluded from the first group of countries to form a single European currency and on lingering concern that the Bundesbank does not want a weaker mark, experts said.

Dollar/yen eased after a senior Japanese financial official warned the era of record low interest rates in Japan may be coming to an end, and a report showed the soft yen was aiding Japanese car makers at the expense of U.S. firms, they said.

Market News Service cited unnamed officials of the German Christian Democratic Union party as saying French President Jacques Chirac was withdrawing support for Italy in its drive to become a founding member of European monetary union (EMU).
But a source in the French government later denied the report, and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi reiterated Italy wants to be in the initial group of nations.
"I think it (concern about Italy) reintroduces skepticism of a broader EMU start, and in general, will raise EMU tensions a little bit," said Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International.

"And given the weakness that we've seen in the deutschemark over the past week, (concern about Italy) provides a little bit more of a reason, I think, to cover short-deutschemark positions," Lynch said.
The dollar closed at 1.7115/20 marks and 125.84/89 yen, down from 1.7160/70 marks and 125.90/95 yen at the open.
The mark's gains versus the yen also helped strengthen the German currency against the dollar.
A trader at the New York branch of a German bank termed the weaker dollar/mark exchange rate a "victim" of the mark's advance against the other currencies.
In late U.S. trade the mark dealt at 73.50 yen, up from around 73.30 in early dealings and an overnight low at 72.95.

During a news conference on Thursday, Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the central bank does not want a weak mark and remains interested in having a strong mark. This statement also continued to weigh on the dollar relative to the mark, experts said.

In an interview with Reuters Financial Television in Tokyo on Friday, senior Japanese Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara warned of the danger in assuming Japanese interest rates will remain at record-low levels over the coming year.

Sakakibara, director-general of the Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau, also put currency markets on notice that a round of central bank dollar sales for yen was possible if Japanese authorities concluded their currency had fallen too far.
Sakakibara's statements "were clearly designed to raise the issues that would undermine the dollar over the long run," said Brian McCarthy, a market analyst at Ruesch International.
"All these things and the messenger certainly weighed on the dollar at the end of the week," he added.
